b: Illness is a heavy burden to carry alone.
Feelings of alienation and illness often go hand in hand.
Social support can ease the pain of loneliness.
Having your life well-peopled can help you live longer.

We all know loneliness is painful on so many levels. Imagine how painful it is when you are ill and possibly dealing with a life-threatening diagnosis and that experience is coupled with loneliness. That is a difficult coupling. In an attempt to address the effect of loneliness on poor health, Rokach & Sha'ked (2015) reviewed research that focused on illness and loneliness. Perhaps you are dealing with this in some area of your life. Sadly, many of us will experience serious illness in our life and/or in the lives of those we love and care about.

Rokach and Sh'ked (2015) reviewed research that found that individuals who had a strong social support group had better immune systems. Loneliness and social isolation appear to be risk factors contributing to illness and may be as risky as elevated blood pressure, smoking, lack of exercise, and obesity. Individuals with more intact social support systems were more likely to live longer. Sadly, lonely people were significantly more likely to die than the well supported.

Regarding the influence of loneliness on the mental health of those awaiting cancer diagnoses, the findings are also quite profound. In at least one study, women waiting for the results of breast biopsies felt significantly more distressed when feeling alone as they lived with ambiguity as they waited for what could possibly be a life-threatening diagnosis. Those awaiting the results of screening for prostate cancer experience similar distress and often feel alienated and as if their day-to-day-life is on hold. Imagine the anxiety and alienation cancer patients must feel if they seek to keep their experiences private. And often there is a tendency to keep this information provide due to all sorts of feelings.

And let us not forget the dying. They are dealing with a range of end-of-life issues. Let us not forget that those receiving palliative care to lessen their pain also have a need for human connection. There is nothing that compares to the experience of being loved and to love in return.

Sadly, there is often a tendency to avoid those who are ill because we are not sure what to say. This is not uncommon. I have frequently heard from those who say that they just don't know what to say. To those individuals I suggest that they don't need to focus as much on their words as they do on being present in the lives of those friends and relatives. These individuals are not defined by their illness. Engage them in discussion of all aspects of their lives. Keep them involved in all sorts of discussions. Take your cues from them about how much they want to disclose about their health. My guess is that they will feel grateful for your continued contact and for offers to accompany them to screenings and even treatment. And listen to them cry. You don't need to—and actually shouldn't—tell them that they are going to be fine. You don't know that and frankly it's a dismissive comment.

If you are dealing with an illness and would like to have certain friends and family involved in your life, please let them know. This will likely make all aspects of your journey easier. Illness is a heavy burden and should not be carried alone.
Rokach, A. & Sh'ked, A. (2015) Ill health, death and loneliness: Mankind's Companions. The Open Psychology Journal.
